  beard. He climbed the rocks to thank her.

  "Saw your light just in time," he said. "Funny thing. My boy drowned out here twenty years ago. On
  nights like that I always feel like he's guiding me home."

  After he left, Mara finally opened the envelope.

  [0m[2m▎[0m [2m[0m[3mYou've[0m [3mmet[0m [3mhim[0m [3mby[0m [3mnow,[0m [3mI[0m [3mexpect.[0m [3mHe[0m [3mdoesn't[0m [3mwant[0m [3manything[0m [3mexcept[0m [3mfor[0m [3mhis[0m [3mfather[0m [3mto[0m [3mget[0m [3mhome[0m [3msafe.

  [0m[2m▎
  [0m[2m▎[0m [2m[0m[3m—[0m [3mE.

  [0m[1mV.[0m [1mThe[0m [1mLast[0m [1mWinter

  Mara stayed through that winter, and the next, and the one after that. She planted her seeds in the
  sheltered side of the rock, and they grew stubbornly in the salt air. Every foggy night she listened
  for the knocking, and she always answered it.

  In the fourth spring the old captain didn't come. A letter arrived instead: he had retired and moved
  inland to be near his sister.

  That night the fog rolled in. Mara waited at the bottom of the stairs until dawn, but nobody
  knocked.

  [0m[1mVI.[0m [1mFor[0m [1mWhoever[0m [1mComes[0m [1mNext

  Before she left, Mara wound the clockwork one last time and set a fresh envelope on the desk. On it
  she wrote [0m[3mFor[0m [3mwhoever[0m [3mcomes[0m [3mnext.

  Inside she put a packet of seeds and a single line:

  [0m[2m▎[0m [2m[0m[3mAnswer[0m [3mthe[0m [3mdoor.[0m [3mSomeone[0m [3mis[0m [3malways[0m [3mtrying[0m [3mto[0m [3mget[0m [3mhome.

  ---

  [0m[3mThe[0m [3mEnd.
